title: Divide and Contrast: Learning Robust Temporal Features without Augmentation
claim: Our method reaches the highest accuracy at low training cost, beating slower or less accurate alternatives on the accuracy–time trade-off.
layout: 1 panel bubble scatter, accuracy vs time, ours highlighted top-left in bold
description: A single scatter plot with training time in hours on the x-axis (0 to 12) and average accuracy in percent on the y-axis (about 67 to 76). Each method is a large, distinctly colored circle with its name beside it. The proposed method, Di-COT (ours), is a blue circle in the top-left corner, labeled in bold. It has the highest accuracy, about 76.4, at a low training time of about 3 hours. Most baselines cluster around 72 to 73.5% accuracy and 3 to 5 hours. TF-C and TNC sit further right at higher cost without higher accuracy. SimMTM is at the bottom right, with the lowest accuracy and over 10 hours. The supervised baseline is at the far left, with low time and about 70% accuracy. Light grid lines run behind the circles. The eye goes first to the isolated blue circle at the top.
caption: Average accuracy vs. training time comparison. Ac- curacy is averaged over five seeds and six large-scale datasets (> 20k samples). Training time denotes the cumulative training time across all six datasets. For SSL methods, encoders are pretrained on the full training set and evaluated with a frozen backbone and a linear probe trained on 1% of the training data, while the supervised baseline is trained end-to-end on 1% labeled data.
abstract: Self-supervised learning for time-series representation aims to reduce reliance on labeled data while maintaining strong downstream performance, yet many existing approaches incur high computational costs or rely on assumptions that do not hold across diverse temporal dynamics. In this work, we introduce Divide and Contrast (Di-COT), an unsupervised framework that avoids data augmentation and multiple encoder passes by contrasting informative substructures within a window rather than individual timesteps. Di-COT stochastically partitions each window into a small number of overlapping sub-blocks per iteration, enabling efficient and meaningful contrast while mitigating false positives during temporal transitions. To further improve scalability, we adopt a contrastive objective whose computation depends on the batch size and the number of sub-blocks, making loss computation independent of sequence length. Extensive experiments on six large-scale real-world datasets, as well as the UCR and UEA benchmarks, demonstrate that Di-COT learns semantically structured and transferable representations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on classification, clustering, $k$NN, and cross-dataset transfer, while substantially reducing training time. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sfi-norwai/Di-COT.
